paras: The reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts was a June 1881 episode in which, according to wire dispatches, fifteen to twenty armed men took four men from their homes in or near Sharp County, Arkansas, one Thursday night and tortured them in a glen to make them confess a robbery. Dispatches from Little Rock said Tibbetts and Stanley could not be found and were feared to have been tortured to death, while the other two men were jailed on suspicion of the robbery. Three weeks later the Sharp County Record denied that anything of the kind had happened in its part of the state.

The affair began, the dispatches said, with the robbery of a "miserly" old farmer named Stokes, given as Thomas Stokes in two versions, who was supposed to keep money hidden about his house. A Little Rock dispatch of June 22 said masked men broke down his doors about midnight, bound the family to chairs, gagged them and rode off with four or five hundred dollars in gold and silver. The robbery "created considerable excitement," and neighbors threatened to hunt the robbers down.

On Thursday night, by the June 20 dispatches, a body of fifteen to twenty armed men went to the homes of James Tibbetts, Abner Stanley and two brothers living near Stokes and carried them to an adjacent glen. There the four were tortured "in a horrible manner" by men who alleged they were the thieves and knew where the money was hidden. Two of them were hung until nearly dead, and all four protested their innocence, according to the fuller Memphis Appeal account.

Tibbetts and Stanley were not seen afterward, and their deaths were reported only as rumor, on the ground that they could not be found. None of the reports gave the race of the four men or of the band that seized them.

The two brothers were arrested on suspicion of the robbery, and the June 22 account placed them in jail at Forsyth, Missouri, charged with robbery. The same account said warrants were out for Stanley and Tibbetts and for all the men who took part in the torture. No report of an arrest of the band, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story moved as a Little Rock special dated June 20, printed by the Chicago Daily Tribune and the Memphis Daily Appeal on June 21 and relayed through St. Louis and New Orleans. The Appeal headed it "Tortured to Death" and "The Latest Arkansas Horror," the Daily Republican ran it as "Lynch Law," and the Stark County Democrat in Ohio as "Four Men Tortured and Made to Confess Murder." Through St. Louis the story reached western papers such as the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Salt Lake Herald on June 22, and the Somerset Herald in Pennsylvania a week later. In retelling the story hardened: the Las Vegas Gazette added that Stokes had been murdered, and the Arizona Miner stated flatly that Tibbetts and Stanley were tortured to death.

The Chicago Tribune ended its special by calling the men seized "reputable citizens," and the Appeal of June 23 ran a fuller account headed "Tortured to Extort a Confession." On July 14 the Sharp County Record reprinted the story from the Athens (Tenn.) Post and called it a "yarn." It said nothing had happened there to support the tale and that a man named Stokes near Evening Shade had not been robbed.

Accounts differed on the brothers' names: James and Johnathan Callahan in the Appeal of June 21, James and John McCallahan in the Chicago Tribune and the Appeal of June 23, and John and Thomas McClanahan in the New Orleans version. They also differed on place, from Sharp County to "the border of Sharp County" to a farm on the line between Arkansas and Missouri, and on timing, since the June 22 dispatch put the robbery on Thursday night and the torture "a few nights ago." The Record's denial rested on a Stokes near Evening Shade, while the June 22 dispatch put its Stokes on the Missouri line; the coverage does not show whether they were the same man.

reader.title: Reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Wire reports described a band of fifteen to twenty armed men seizing four men accused of a robbery and torturing and hanging them to force a confession, two said to have died (A1, A2, A3, A9); the local paper denied it happened (A14).

The reports describe an extralegal band of 15-20 men torturing robbery suspects, but the deaths of Tibbetts and Stanley were only 'said' or 'feared' because they could not be found (A2, A3, A9), and the Sharp County Record denied the whole story (A14); no report confirms a death.
Several distinct wire versions agree on the core story (A1, A2, A3, A9), but the local Sharp County Record called it a fabrication and said the Stokes it knew had not been robbed (A14).

accounts.gist: Six masked men robbed Stokes; on Thursday night 15-20 armed men tortured four neighbors in a glen; the Callahans were arrested and Tibbetts and Stanley were said to have been tortured to death since they could not be found.

accounts.label: New Orleans version
accounts.gist: Names the brothers John and Thomas McClanahan; the four were hung until nearly dead; the McClanahans were jailed and Tibbetts and Stanley feared murdered.

accounts.label: Little Rock dispatch, June 22
accounts.gist: Places Stokes on the Arkansas-Missouri line; two men hung until nearly dead, all protested innocence; the McCallahans jailed at Forsyth, Missouri, and warrants out for Stanley, Tibbetts and the band.

accounts.label: Sharp County Record (local denial)
accounts.gist: Nothing of the kind happened in that part of the state; a Stokes near Evening Shade had not been robbed and was not a miser.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Tortured to Death... The Latest Arkansas Horror' (Memphis Appeal) and 'Lynch Law' (Daily Republican) presented the torture as an outrage.
The Chicago Tribune's special ended by calling the men seized 'reputable citizens'.
Western and Ohio papers ran the St. Louis Republican and Little Rock wire under 'Horrible', 'Arkansas Horrors' and 'Four Men Tortured and Made to Confess Murder'.
The Sharp County Record ridiculed the story as a 'yarn' invented by a 'liar' and denied anything had happened.
